scenario: Today's personalization track asks who should be able to see and change the signals in a recommender, and where limited budget should be spent. One line keeps a long behavior history at full resolution for unified ranking and sees higher merchandise value in advertising traffic; another turns natural-language interests into editable serving addresses, so people can direct retrieval and exposure. A multimodal paper first lets a large model write coarse and fine features, then fuses them in the middle of a graph network, while an uplift model for promotional pricing warns that product text may leak the treatment decision. Others treat a newly opened location as an intervention on a district's return, use a simple rule to find patients more likely to benefit from home blood-pressure telemonitoring, and first decide whether an edit suggestion should be shown in a conversation. Product entity resolution, feature algebra, and live EEG music recommendation each make the same practical point: match the structure to data noise, efficiency goals, and the mood of the moment, rather than defaulting to the heaviest model.

papers.title: TokenFormer V2: Breaking the Resolution-Complexity Dilemma in Unified Recommendation
papers.authors: Kaihui Wu, Guoming Li, Liang Guo, Yifeng Zhou, Yuehong Hu, Junwei Pan, Zhixiang Feng, Chengguo Yin, Wenqi Fan, Haijie Gu, Jie Jiang
papers.summary: Industrial recommenders need fine-grained long behavior histories, yet they must stay inside a strict serving budget: keeping every event is expensive, and compact summaries throw evidence away. This work decouples representation resolution from interaction density. It encodes behaviors in local groups, expands range through hierarchical merging and global synchronization, and still lets the final predictor read every encoded event directly. On the Tencent Advertising Algorithm Competition public benchmark, AUC rises 0.10 percentage points over MixFormer, the strongest unified backbone, while forward FLOPs are only 19.5% of that baseline. The lead remains on longer and more imbalanced histories. In a live traffic test on WeChat Channels ads, GMV rises a statistically significant 2.33% over the production model. ==Fine-grained history does not have to be compressed before it can fit the budget==. For teams choosing a unified ranking backbone, this is an organization already tested online.
papers.abstract: Industrial recommendation faces a resolution--complexity dilemma: dense interactions make detailed modeling of long behavior histories expensive, while compact history summaries restrict the evidence available to prediction. A unified backbone must preserve rich behavioral details within strict serving budgets. We introduce \textbf{TokenFormer V2}, a unified architecture that explicitly decouples \emph{representation resolution} from \emph{interaction density}. Its group-wise token layout jointly encodes behavior segments with non-sequential context, expands interaction ranges via hierarchical group merging, and coordinates distributed groups through \emph{NS Fusion} and \emph{Global Sync} modules. Through this \emph{local--global decomposition} paradigm, computation is concentrated on structured interactions while preserving fine-grained evidence, ensuring that every encoded event remains directly accessible to the \emph{Full-Resolution Readout} module. On the Tencent Advertising Algorithm Competition 2026 (TAAC 2026) benchmark, TokenFormer V2 achieves top-ranking accuracy among unified recommendation baselines while using \textbf{5.1$\times$ fewer FLOPs} than leading baselines, sustaining its advantage across long histories and imbalanced behavior domains. Furthermore, in billion-parameter evaluations on WeChat Channels advertising, it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art industrial baselines, yielding up to a \textbf{+0.07 pp} overall AUC gain. In live online A/B testing against the production model, TokenFormer V2 delivers a statistically significant \textbf{2.33\% increase in GMV}. These results establish TokenFormer V2 as a battle-tested blueprint for scalable, full-resolution behavior modeling in industrial recommendation.

papers.title: CLEAR: Legible and Steerable Recommendation via Grounded Natural-Language Interests
papers.authors: Qi Guo, Reza Mirghaderi, Iordanis Fostiropoulos, David Fan, Yuchen Liu, Shiliang Tang, Lukasz Korycki, Golnaz Ghasemiesfeh, Xinzhu Bei, Sasha Vorontsov, Hanchao Yu, Brendan Quinlivan, Khoi Pham, Jigar Gada, Hao Yu, Felix Li, Hang Gao, Boyu Fang, Yang Gao, Yale Thomas, Xiaomeng Jin, Avishek Dutta, Hong Hong, Janet Xia, Ethan Zhu, Ellie Pan, Xiang Shen, Jawwad Zakaria, Jinfeng Lin, Jonathan Rush, Ruixue Lian, Noah Kennedy, Brian Vanover, Jas Pyneni, Daniel Thiyagu, Apoorv Saxena, Sanyogeeta Lawande, Huayu Ding, Hima Cherukuru, Yang Liu, Chen Kovacs, Qunshu Zhang, Lizhu Zhang, Benyu Zhang, Kate Chen, Ashish Singal, Danny Kanoff, Zhiyu Liu, Jiayi Liu, Jianyu Wang, Fei Liu, Xiangjun Fan, Abhishek Kumar, Hong Yan
papers.summary: Recommenders often bury user taste in hidden vectors that people cannot inspect or change, so adding or suppressing an interest usually has no handle. CLEAR, deployed at Meta, adds an editable natural-language interest layer: each interest is grounded in the user's own history and serves as an address for retrieval, ranking, and exposure control. A newly declared interest can enter the candidate set through topical retrieval even before behavioral support exists. In direct user review, about 88.5% of displayed interests were rated accurate. For a newly declared interest, removing interest-conditioned candidate sourcing in the tested sequence cut same-day delivery by 13.7 percentage points. Components have run in production for more than a year across four surfaces on Instagram and Facebook. ==An interest has to be readable and able to change what gets ranked==. For products that want people to direct recommendations, this hooks a legible interest layer into the existing serving path.
papers.abstract: Modern recommenders keep learned preferences in representations people cannot inspect or change. We present CLEAR (Controllable and Legible End-to-end Architecture for Recommendation), an end-to-end system deployed at Meta and built around an editable natural-language interest layer. CLEAR makes a ranked subset of inferred interests readable and stores accepted additions and suppressions as authoritative preference state. Behavioral grounding maps each inferred interest back to supporting events in the user's own history. The resulting interest object is also a serving address: its label and profile-conditioned rewrites drive lexical retrieval, its supporting events seed behavioral retrieval, its projection queries an embedding index, and its stable identity supports ranking, attribution, and exposure control. A fresh user declaration may precede behavioral support, so it enters through the same serving identity and initially draws candidates from topical retrieval. Ranking makes those candidates competitive, while a delivery controller observes attributable exposure and replenishes underexposed interests. Direct user review found that users rated about 88.5% of displayed interests accurate. In an offline benchmark using a shared evaluation protocol, the Specialized 3B generator reached 0.3967 mean-user F1@10, compared with 0.3633 for Gemini 2.5 Pro and 0.1911 for the prior generator. For a newly declared interest, a user-randomized cumulative ablation measured same-day delivery losses of 8.7 percentage points for added-interest ranking terms, 11.1 for reserved top-slot insertion, and 13.7 for interest-conditioned candidate sourcing, conditional on the tested removal sequence. CLEAR components have operated in production for over one year; the system spans four surfaces on Instagram and Facebook, with an interest layer people can inspect, correct, and use to direct recommendations.

papers.title: Take a Step Back: A Dual-Granularity Raw Feature Empowered Intermediate Fusion Graph Convolutional Network for Multimodal Recommendation
papers.authors: Jinfeng Xu, Zheyu Chen, Shuo Yang, Jinze Li, Wenhao Yuan, Ziyue Peng, Puzhen Wu, Shujie Li, Jian Chen, Zheng Lin, Edith C. H. Ngai
papers.summary: Multimodal recommenders try to learn multi-level representations from sparse interactions, and often use contrastive learning to align modalities, which can squeeze out information that is unique to one modality. This work suggests taking a step back: large models generate coarse and fine raw features before training, as a complement to the original item features, rather than replacing the original text and images. An intermediate-fusion graph convolution network with dynamic cross-modality weight correction then captures cross-modality signals, instead of first forcing every modality into the same direction. On four standard Amazon datasets, Recall@20 rises 3.54% to 8.81% relative to MambaRec, the strongest baseline, and the gains remain under higher sparsity and item cold start. The model can also still benefit from additional alignment tasks. For graph-based multimodal recommenders, granularity need not be learned only from sparse interactions, and fusion need not rely on alignment alone.
papers.abstract: Although multimodal recommendations have shown the ability to learn user preferences and item properties by leveraging explicit multimodal information, they remain constrained by two critical limitations: low-quality representation learning and modality fusion. For the former, existing solutions primarily focus on multi-granularity representation learning; however, we argue that training such representations is difficult due to the inherent data sparsity problem in recommendation scenarios. For the latter, existing solutions often rely on contrastive learning to align representations of different modalities to facilitate modality fusion, yet alignment-only objectives may over-compress valuable modality-specific information. To this end, we suggest \underline{``Take a Step Back"} and propose a \textbf{D}ual-granularity raw feature empowered \textbf{I}ntermediate fusion \textbf{G}raph \textbf{C}onvolutional \textbf{N}etwork (\textbf{DIGCN}) for multimodal recommendation. DIGCN leverages the multimodal understanding capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to construct dual-granularity raw features directly. Furthermore, DIGCN introduces an intermediate fusion graph convolutional network equipped with dynamic cross-modality weight correction, designed to capture cross-modality signals and achieve effective modality fusion. Comprehensive experiments on four real-world datasets validate that DIGCN consistently outperforms a variety of strong baselines. Additional analyses confirm its superiority under varying levels of data sparsity and cold-start scenarios. Notably, DIGCN demonstrates high extensibility, capable of further benefiting from additional contrastive learning-based alignment tasks.

papers.title: Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation
papers.authors: Bojing Feng, Jinqiu Deng, Zihan Hong, Yuan Xue, Wenqi Xiang, Shuhan Wang, Feng Xiao, Shiwei Wang, Zijiang Liu, Shaomin Li, Yongzhi Qi
papers.summary: When a large model reads product text to estimate the uplift of promotional pricing, titles may already contain words such as “clearance” that reveal the treatment decision. The model can take that shortcut, then fail when a real decision is still pending and the text does not yet carry those words. LULR freezes the encoder and adds a mutual-information penalty on the causal head's shared representation, to reduce dependence between that representation and the treatment. On a million-record industrial pricing randomized trial, the offline metric was better in four of five random seeds, but the difference was not statistically significant and policy values were nearly tied. In a separate one-week online test, the complete deployed pricing policy had 5.45% higher sales volume and 1.91% higher GMV than the control group. That is short-term business evidence for the full policy, and it does not isolate the regularizer. For teams feeding product text into an uplift model, blocking treatment leakage matters more than simply adding more text.
papers.abstract: Uplift modeling estimates the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and supports industrial decisions such as promotional pricing. When large language models (LLMs) encode product text, treatment-revealing content can introduce shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose \emph{LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization} (\textsc{LULR}), which uses a CLUB-based penalty on the causal head's trainable shared representation while keeping the LLM encoder frozen. Controlled proxy experiments show a positive ranking-score interaction and higher scores than the tested weight-decay configuration; treatment-dependent evaluation limits their interpretation to exploratory model behavior. Structured-only comparisons provide reference performance, without establishing a general advantage over tree-based estimators. On a million-record industrial pricing RCT, \textsc{LULR} improves offline $\text{lift@}0.3$ in $4/5$ seeds, although the difference is not statistically significant and estimated policy values are near-tied. A separate one-week online A/B experiment records $5.45\%$ higher sales volume and $1.91\%$ higher GMV than the control arm. These aggregate results provide short-term business evidence for the complete deployed pricing policy; they do not isolate the regularizer's contribution.

papers.title: Real-World End-to-End Product Entity Resolution
papers.authors: Dimitrios Karapiperis, George Papadakis, Manolis Koubarakis
company: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens
papers.summary: Matching the same product across e-commerce catalogs is hard: titles mix promotional wording and messy formatting, and many near-lookalikes actually come from different brands. This evaluation compares four zero-shot cascades built from lexical, semantic, and hybrid retrieval plus generative verification, and releases RETAILERS, a real-world dataset with cross-lingual noise and dense brand collisions. No single architecture wins on every dataset: lexical retrieval is faster and lighter on short titles, while semantic retrieval handles wording changes better but also pulls in same-brand near-lookalikes. On the noisier RETAILERS-D split, hybrid retrieval plus remote GPT verification reaches an F1 of 0.666 and is about 34 times faster than local Gemma. A cross-encoder is a more practical default matcher, while a large model fits accuracy-critical or smaller-scale settings better. For product entity resolution, choose the cascade from the data noise and the latency budget, rather than defaulting to the heaviest generative verifier.
papers.abstract: Product Entity Resolution (PER) in e-commerce is challenging due to unstructured text, formatting inconsistencies, promotional noise, and fine-grained product differences. We present an end-to-end evaluation of four zero-shot PER pipelines---Lexical Cascade, Semantic Cascade, Hybrid Fusion Cascade, and Generative-Lexical Cascade---across established benchmarks and introduce two real-world datasets characterized by cross-lingual noise and dense brand collisions. We evaluate lexical and dense blocking with cross-encoder, tensor-search, and Large Language Model verification, considering accuracy, runtime, and memory consumption.

papers.title: UrbanROI: Causal Modeling for Regional ROI Forecasting under POI Entry
papers.authors: Zhaoqi Zhang, Miao Xie, Linyou Cai, Qianlong Xie, Xingxing Wang, Siqiang Luo, Gao Cong
papers.summary: When a new point of interest opens in a commercial area, it can change the region's advertising or business return, but common forecasts watch a single store or one time series. They do not model competition among nearby locations, and they cannot separate the path if nothing had opened from the gain that comes with entry. UrbanROI builds a regional graph from user requests, spatial proximity, and request-level commercial signals, and constructs treated and control graphs for the entered and unentered states. Removing the regional graph or the causal decomposition both hurts accuracy. On real data from Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, and Guangzhou, it beats the strongest baseline on every error metric. In a semi-synthetic effect-recovery test, sign accuracy rises from 71.2% with temporal information only to 85.0%. For regional ads and merchant onboarding, treat a new location as an intervention, rather than fitting one more accurate curve.
papers.abstract: As urban commercial environments continue to evolve rapidly, accurately modeling the economic impact of point of interest (POI) entry is essential for supporting data-driven advertising allocation, merchant onboarding, and regional business decision-making. Existing return on investment (ROI) prediction methods mainly focus on individual ads or merchants, overlooking the interaction effects among POIs and failing to capture the causal influence of structural changes in urban commercial ecosystems. In this paper, we introduce a novel research problem -- regional ROI forecasting under POI entry, which aims to predict the future ROI trajectory of a commercial region after the introduction of a new POI by modeling temporal ROI evolution and competition-driven interactions among surrounding POIs. To address these challenges, we propose UrbanROI, an intervention-aware causal forecasting framework for region-level economic outcome prediction. UrbanROI leverages an Interaction-aware Regional Graph Module to explicitly model competitive relationships among POIs based on user request contexts, spatial proximity, and request-level commercial signals, and constructs structurally aligned treatment and control graphs to simulate factual and counterfactual regional states. Extensive experiments on large-scale real-world POI and advertising datasets demonstrate that UrbanROI consistently outperforms strong baselines in post-entry regional ROI forecasting. The results demonstrate its effectiveness in temporal economic modeling, inter-POI interaction representation, and intervention-aware forecasting, providing support for regional economic analysis and business decision-making in dynamic urban commercial systems.

papers.title: Edit Recommendation: Can LLMs Anticipate Edit Requests from Users, and When?
papers.summary: After a large model writes an email or a passage, users often send edit requests. Anticipating those requests before they arrive would cut a round of review, but some real edits introduce information that is absent from the prior context, such as a new name, constraint, or goal, and are inherently hard to predict. This work builds a benchmark from WildChat conversation logs and adds decision-model gating: it filters cases that are unlikely to be correct before suggestions are shown. At one gating threshold, the trained model raises the share of shown five-suggestion lists that contain a hit by 12 to 25 percentage points, and the gain also holds for predictors that were not used in training. ==Edit suggestions should not be pushed after every reply==. For teams recommending edits in a chat, deciding when to show a suggestion is more practical than only chasing a higher hit rate.
papers.abstract: After a large language model (LLM) agent generates an artifact, users often send edit requests for it. This paper studies whether an LLM can anticipate these requests before they are sent. Such anticipation is useful in practice because it reduces the effort of user review and feedback. We formalize this task as edit recommendation and build EditRecBench, a benchmark for evaluating the performance of LLMs on this task, from real-world conversation logs in WildChat-4.8M. Through benchmarking and failure analysis, we identify a practical challenge that some cases are inherently difficult to predict in real-world settings. To address this, we introduce decision model-based gating to filter out cases where predictions are unlikely to be correct before they are presented to the user. Our trained model outperforms existing decision models and raises pass@5 among shown suggestions by 12--25 points at a gating threshold. Our code is available at https://github.com/ntt-dkiku/llm-edit-recommendation.

papers.title: Algebraic Interaction: A Recipe for Neural Architecture Generation
papers.summary: Convolution, attention, and state-space models are usually rewritten as one undivided mechanism, so a change in efficiency or symmetry often means rebuilding both the information pathway and the feature interaction. This work expresses them as bilinear products over a position algebra and a feature algebra, so the original information pathway can stay fixed while only the feature interaction changes. Replacing the feature algebra in Vision Mamba with a structure-constant algebra avoids a large matrix-valued hidden state, speeds training and inference by about 3 times, and keeps CIFAR-10 accuracy at 86.350%, close to the original 86.818%. Linear attention also gains accuracy at a comparable parameter count, and an algebra of three-dimensional rotation representations supplies rotational equivariance by construction. For people designing network architectures, the feature algebra is itself a design variable; positional routing does not have to be rebuilt first.
papers.abstract: We introduce an algebraic foundation for neural architecture design in which convolution, attention, state-space models, and equivariant layers are expressed through compositions of bilinear product operators over two structures: a position algebra governing positional routing and a feature algebra governing feature interactions. This decomposition makes routing, feature algebra, and operator composition explicit design variables.We focus on the feature-algebra axis through an Algebraic Recipe: fix the routing and operator composition of an existing architecture while replacing its feature algebra. This preserves the information-flow structure while allowing computational and symmetry properties to be modified through algebraic specification.We instantiate the recipe in linear attention, Mamba, and equivariant networks. Structure-constant and Clifford algebras improve accuracy at comparable parameter count in linear attention; structure-constant algebras yield up to $3\times$ faster training and inference in Vision Mamba at competitive accuracy; and an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-representation algebra provides rotational equivariance by construction. These results demonstrate that feature algebra alone can control accuracy, efficiency, and symmetry without redesigning positional routing.This turns algebraic structure into an explicit design variable and reduces architecture design, within our framework, to algebraic specification.

papers.title: EE-Motion: An EEG-based Web Architecture for Live Affective Music Recommendation
papers.authors: Sabino Roccotelli, Potito Aghilar, Vito Walter Anelli, Alejandro Bellogín, Tommaso Colafiglio, Michelantonio Trizio, Tommaso Di Noia
papers.summary: Mood drifts continuously in a single listening session, but recommenders still lean on static profiles and offline training, and they struggle to serve anonymous visitors who have no history and cannot be retrained on the spot. This web system pairs a consumer EEG headband with the browser over Bluetooth, maps frontal alpha asymmetry and an arousal index onto a valence-arousal plane, and uses an affective adapter to score diverse backbones, including graph networks and sequential Transformers, from the live coordinates. An anonymous visitor only picks a few favorite tracks, with no user table. Without a headband, a cursor on the same plane still shows how the ranking moves with the coordinates. In a local test, ACE and SASRec with the adapter both finish a cycle well below the 125 millisecond deadline of an 8 hertz EEG stream, so requests do not queue up. Signals stay in session memory and are deleted afterwards, and they are not used as a clinical mood diagnosis.
papers.abstract: Music listening is intrinsically tied to emotion, which drifts continuously within a single session. Although modern browsers interface with wearable brain-computer interfaces, recommendation systems remain structured around discrete logs and lack the infrastructure to integrate continuous physiological signals. Furthermore, existing affect-aware models rely on static user profiles and offline training, failing to serve anonymous newcomers without model retraining. We present a web platform that resolves both challenges. Pairing with a consumer electroencephalogram (EEG) headband over Web Bluetooth, the system captures live EEG, mapping frontal alpha asymmetry and arousal index to normalized valence-arousal proxy coordinates on Russell's circumplex plane. Driven by these coordinates, an affective adapter unifies structurally diverse recommendation backbones under a shared live scoring mechanism. By parameterizing anonymous visitors through a few favorite tracks, the module recommends tracks conditioned on live proxy coordinates. This demonstrates that real-time EEG-derived control signals can steer recommendations without persistent user tables or model retraining.

papers.title: Who Benefits from Telemonitoring? Uplift Modelling of a Nationwide Home Blood Pressure Monitoring Programme
papers.summary: Home blood-pressure telemonitoring is now a national programme, but devices and follow-up staff are limited, and the benefit is unlikely to be the same for every patient. A hypertension telemonitoring programme in Singapore used propensity-score matching on more than sixteen thousand enrolled patients: the six-month blood-pressure control rate rose 5 percentage points overall, and 12 percentage points among those whose blood pressure was not controlled at baseline. Individual uplift estimates then suggested larger gains for people with a higher baseline blood-pressure grade, a more recent diagnosis, and a lower medication and diagnosis burden, and realized gains were also larger at the top of the predicted-uplift ranking. A simple rule written from those features even outperformed every learned model on the uncontrolled-baseline subgroup. That is a usable clue for writing enrolment criteria when care capacity is scarce, though the estimates are still imprecise and not fully cleared of confounding.
papers.abstract: Home blood pressure (BP) telemonitoring programmes are being deployed at national scale, yet enrolment resources are finite and the benefit of telemonitoring is unlikely to be uniform across patients. We study the Primary Technology-Enhanced Care for Hypertension (PTEC-HT) programme, a nationwide telemonitoring programme for hypertensive patients in Singapore. Using retrospective data on 16,694 patients registered between August 2020 and May 2024, we first estimate the average treatment effect of the programme on 6-month BP control against a propensity-score-matched non-participant cohort, finding an absolute improvement of 5 percentage points in the rate of BP control (74% vs. 69%, $p = 3\times10^{-12}$), rising to 12 percentage points (63% vs. 50%, $p = 1\times10^{-15}$) among patients with uncontrolled BP at baseline. We then move beyond the average effect and apply uplift modelling to estimate individual treatment effects. Across five uplift learners evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation and Qini curves, an uplift random forest performed best on the full cohort and an S-learner on the uncontrolled-baseline subcohort, although performance bands overlapped across learners. On held-out patients, realised uplift was largest in the top predicted-uplift groups and declined across the ranking. These patients had higher baseline BP grade, more recent hypertension diagnosis and lower medication and diagnosis burden, a profile we offer as hypothesis-generating for targeted enrolment. A handcrafted rule built from these features was competitive with the learned models, outperforming all of them on the uncontrolled-baseline cohort, suggesting that uplift models are useful for discovering heterogeneity that can be distilled into simple enrolment criteria for directing limited care team capacity.
